design_detail: Short communication (European Psychiatry 16:127-130): a retrospective structured-interview survey, by authors at Geha Psychiatric Hospital, Petah Tikva, and Tel Aviv University, Israel, of 20 men and 15 women who had occasionally used MDMA before a sexual encounter (9 of the 35 interviewed by telephone). Each person rated sexual activity up to 6 hours after taking MDMA against their usual sexual function without it, for desire, erection (lubrication in women), orgasm intensity, orgasm delay and satisfaction, on a scale from -3 (marked decrease) to +3 (marked increase). Results are descriptive percentages plus a table of every participant's age, education and ratings (Table I); no statistical tests or intervals are printed. Recruitment method, place and dates of the interviews are not stated (received by the journal 11 October 1999).
can_establish: How these 35 people, recalling sex after taking MDMA, rated their desire, erections or lubrication, orgasm and satisfaction compared with their usual sex without MDMA.
cannot_establish: How common these effects are among people who take MDMA (a self-selected sample, recruited in an unstated way, of people who had used it before sex), whether MDMA itself caused them (no comparison condition, unknown dose and content of the pills, retrospective recall, expectations, and cannabis used with MDMA by 20 of 35), or anything about sexual risk or long-term sexual function.

sample.recruitment: Not described. The paper says only that 20 men and 15 women who had occasionally used MDMA before engaging in a sexual encounter consented to a structured interview (p. 127, Subjects and methods, 1st paragraph); the setting is Israel by the authors' affiliation.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included only people who were physically healthy, without a major psychiatric disorder or history of sexual disorders, medication-free and, in the paper's word, not abusing alcohol or opiates; all had prior recreational experience with MDMA; the same criteria were checked for the 9 telephone interviews (pp. 127-128).
sample.demographics: Ages 21 to 48 (men 22 to 46, women 21 to 48; editors' calculation from Table I: mean 31.1 years for men, 31.7 for women); 94% had a high-school or academic education (33 of 35 had 12 or more years in Table I); six were full-time university students and the rest steadily employed in professional occupations (p. 128; Table I, p. 129).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); the number of people approached or declining is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people willing to describe their use of an illegal drug, all of whom had used MDMA before sex; people with sexual or psychiatric disorders excluded; mostly educated and employed. The authors name the non-random sample, retrospective and possibly inaccurate recall, unknown dose and purity, and cannabis use by about half as limitations (p. 129).

exposure.measurement: Self-report of past MDMA use in a sexual setting; what was taken was not confirmed, and the dose and purity of the pills could not be determined (p. 129).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. Use before sex is described as occasional; number of occasions, amounts and time since the last occasion are not reported; ratings refer to sexual activity up to 6 hours after taking MDMA (pp. 127-128).
exposure.polysubstance: Ten men (50%) and ten women (67%) reported occasional use of cannabis with MDMA, mainly, they said, to enhance desire; ratings were said to be restricted to MDMA alone, and the authors report no differences in any sexual rating between those who did and did not add cannabis, without numbers or tests (p. 128). Alcohol use short of the exclusion criterion is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective interview); time since last use not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Each person compared sex after MDMA with their own usual sexual function without MDMA, from memory.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Usual sexual function was not measured, and relationship status, partners, setting, other substances on the occasions recalled and expectations were not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: A structured interview on four domains (desire; erection in men or lubrication in women; orgasm, assessed for intensity and for ease of achievement; satisfaction), citing the authors' earlier study of amantadine in men with schizophrenia (reference 16) for the domains; each item rated from -3 to +3 against the person's usual function (0 unchanged, 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 profound or marked; minus a decrease, plus an increase) (p. 128; Table I legend, p. 129).
outcomes.validity_norms: No reliability or validity data; an ad hoc rating scale rather than a validated sexual-function questionnaire.
outcomes.operationalization: Moderate to profound increase means a rating of +2 or +3; impaired sexual performance, in the authors' conclusion, means a decrease in erection rating, delayed orgasm or anorgasmia (p. 129).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive only; the one comparison, by cannabis use, is reported without a test).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; who conducted the interviews is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only, without intervals. Editors' tallies from Table I with Wilson 95% intervals (editors' calculation): sexual desire increased in 35 of 35, moderately or markedly in 34 (97%; 85.5% to 99.5%); satisfaction moderately or markedly increased in 32 of 35 (91%; 77.6% to 97.0%); erections worse in 8 of 20 men (40%; 21.9% to 61.3%), 4 of them moderately or markedly, better in 8 (40%) and unchanged in 4; lubrication increased in 12 of 15 women (80%; 54.8% to 93.0%) and decreased in 2; orgasm delayed in 16 of 20 men (80%; 58.4% to 91.9%) and 6 of 15 women (40%; 19.8% to 64.3%); no orgasm at all on MDMA in 1 man and 2 women; orgasm more intense in 17 men (85%) and 8 women (53%), less intense in 1 man and 3 women. All 8 men who reported weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm rated satisfaction as moderately or markedly increased.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned; no ethics committee approval is mentioned, only consent.
analysis.selective_reporting: Every participant's ratings are printed in Table I, so the percentages in the text can be checked (they agree, see reporting issues). The comparison by cannabis use is stated without data, and Table I does not show who used cannabis.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive); with 20 men and 15 women, proportions are uncertain by about 20 percentage points either way (for example 40% of 20 men: 21.9% to 61.3%, editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: All 35 recalled more sexual desire after MDMA and 32 rated satisfaction moderately or markedly higher; 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women recalled delayed orgasm and 3 people could not reach orgasm; 8 of 20 men recalled weaker erections and 8 stronger ones; 12 of 15 women recalled more lubrication; orgasm felt more intense to 17 men and 8 women.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and conclusion say MDMA seems to impair sexual performance in spite of enhanced desire and the perception of greater satisfaction, and that the increased desire is associated in most subjects with orgasmic or erectile dysfunction (pp. 127, 129). The summary reports erections impaired in 40% of the men without the other 40% who reported better erections, which the Discussion calls inconsistent effects (p. 128); and the dysfunction counted is mostly delayed orgasm in people who still rated satisfaction higher (editors' tally from Table I: 17 of 20 men and 8 of 15 women had delayed orgasm, no orgasm or weaker erections or lubrication). The links to dopamine and serotonin are hypotheses not tested here, and the authors themselves say expectations (a placebo effect) should not be disregarded (p. 128).

timeline.event: Buffum and Moser, self-rating questionnaires distributed in the San Francisco area, as cited here as the only earlier survey of MDMA and sexual function: MDMA enhanced sensuality, made orgasm more difficult and decreased erectile ability in 46% of men (p. 128); not read.

McElrath, in-depth interviews with 98 people in Northern Ireland (1997-1998): many described closeness without wanting penetrative sex, some men described being unable to get an erection, and others described heightened desire; no counts given.

replication.where_it_stands: Small self-report studies from the 1980s and 1990s agree that desire and sensuality often rise with MDMA while erections and orgasm can be impaired; no study among those read measured sexual function under controlled conditions or in a representative sample.

funding.affiliations_note: Geha Psychiatric Hospital, Petah Tikva, and Sackler Faculty of Medicine, Tel Aviv University, Israel (p. 127).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective diary study in which people who use MDMA rate sexual function with a validated questionnaire on occasions with and without MDMA, with the pills tested and other substances recorded; or a placebo-controlled laboratory study measuring desire, arousal and orgasm.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame is described; how the 35 people were found is not stated.
Self-selected people who had used MDMA before sex and agreed to talk about it; not a random or consecutive sample.
35 people (20 men, 15 women); intervals around the sex-specific proportions span about 40 percentage points.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex and years of education are given for every person, with occupations summarized; recruitment, place and dates are not described.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 35 participants' ratings are shown in Table I and the text's percentages match it.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: An unvalidated retrospective self-rating scale; the exposure (MDMA) is unverified and its dose and content unknown.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One structured interview for all, but 9 by telephone, interviewers not described and recall over unspecified periods.
Descriptive percentages suit a description, but there are no intervals and the comparison by cannabis use has neither data nor test.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: The number of people approached or declining is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, self-selected, retrospective survey with an unvalidated rating scale and unverified exposure, whose per-person table at least makes every count checkable. It may be cited for what these 35 people recalled: more desire and satisfaction, delayed orgasm in most men, and erections reported as worse by 40% of men but better by another 40%. It should not be cited for how often these effects occur among people who take MDMA, or as showing that MDMA causes them.

key_findings.finding: Sample and method: 35 people (20 men aged 22 to 46, 15 women aged 21 to 48) who had occasionally used MDMA before sex were interviewed retrospectively (9 by telephone) about sexual activity up to 6 hours after MDMA, rating each domain from -3 to +3 against their usual function without MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Summary (p. 127); Subjects and methods, 1st paragraph (p. 127, continuing on p. 128) and 2nd paragraph (p. 128); Table I (p. 129)

key_findings.finding: Desire: all 35 reported increased sexual desire after MDMA; the increase was moderate to profound in 19 of 20 men (95%) and in all 15 women; most described the experience as more sensual than usual.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 128); Table I, title and rows (p. 129)

key_findings.finding: Satisfaction: moderately to profoundly increased in 90% of men and 93% of women (18 of 20 and 14 of 15 in Table I).
Erection: 40% of men (8 of 20) reported a negative effect and 40% (8) a positive effect, and 4 no change; lubrication was enhanced in 80% of women (12 of 15).
key_findings.note: Editors' tally from Table I: of the 8 men with weaker erections, 4 rated the decrease as moderate or marked (-2 or -3); 2 women reported less lubrication.

key_findings.finding: Orgasm: delayed in 16 men (80%) and 6 women (40%); 1 man and 2 women had not been able to reach orgasm at all on MDMA; orgasm was perceived as more intense by 85% of men and 53% of women.
key_findings.note: Editors' tally from Table I: orgasm felt less intense to 1 man and 3 women, 3 of these 4 being the people who could not reach orgasm.

key_findings.finding: Satisfaction stayed high despite impaired function: all 8 men who reported weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm rated satisfaction at +2 or +3.
key_findings.note: Editors' tally from the individual ratings in Table I.

key_findings.finding: Cannabis: 10 men (50%) and 10 women (67%) reported occasional use of cannabis with MDMA, mainly to enhance desire; ratings were restricted to MDMA alone, and the authors report no differences in any sexual rating between those who did and did not add cannabis (no data or test shown).

The authors compare their results with the only earlier survey they knew (Buffum and Moser, 1986, San Francisco area): MDMA enhanced sensuality, made orgasm harder to achieve and decreased erectile ability in 46% of men (as cited).

Limitations named by the authors: a non-random sample of people willing to describe use of an illegal drug, retrospective recall open to inaccuracy, unknown dose and purity of the pills, and cannabis use by about half; they also say expected effects of the drug (a placebo effect) should not be disregarded, citing alcohol studies in which women felt more aroused while measured arousal fell.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary reports erection impaired in 40% of the men, but not that another 40% reported better erections (both in Results, p. 128), and concludes that MDMA impairs sexual performance.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary overstates the erection finding; the Discussion itself calls the effects on erection inconsistent (p. 128).

reporting_issues.issue: Telephone interviews are given as 9 subjects (25%); 9 of 35 is 26% (editors' calculation). All other percentages in the text match the individual ratings in Table I (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible; the counts are reliable as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that sexual ratings did not differ between people who did and did not use cannabis with MDMA is given without numbers or a test, and Table I does not mark who used cannabis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that cannabis did not affect the ratings cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Recruitment method, place and dates of the interviews, the interviewers and ethics approval are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample frame and representativeness cannot be judged (JBI items 1, 2 and 9).

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/MDMA/Zemishlany_2001_MDMASexualFunction.pdf (version of record, as reposted by Cambridge University Press), pp. 127-130, all pages; every page rendered at 150 dpi and Table I re-read at 300 dpi, and the text's percentages recounted from Table I. No supplement.
